newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori calls hostage crisis isolated act.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori calls hostage crisis isolated act.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori said the five-week-old stand-off between his government and Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages in Lima will not revive the ghosts of Peru's bloody past nor threaten free-market reform.

Though Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) gunmen refused to bow to pressure to release their captives, Fujimori insisted on Monday that the hostage crisis was nothing more that an isolated incident.
"The Peruvian people do not want to go backwards nor accept a return of violence and disorder to the country," he said in speeches to welcome two new ambassadors to Peru.
In six years of power, Fujimori virtually defeated leftist guerrillas waging armed conflict since 1980 and transformed the Peruvian economy along free-market lines.
Before the guerrilla movements were suppressed, an estimated 30,000 people were killed after 1980 in conflicts involving the government against the MRTA and larger Maoist Shining Path movements.

But the spectacular Dec. 17 takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence by MRTA rebels claiming to represent the poor, revived memories of Peru's past and threatened to set back Fujimori's achievements.
Local terrorism experts warned last year that despite setbacks at the hands of security forces in recent years, Peru's two guerrilla groups could be preparing for new offensives.
A group of at least 30 Shining Path guerrillas appeared in several villages in central Peru on Monday, police said.
"There were about 30 of them," a spokesman for the DINCOTE antiterrorist police in the central town of Tingo Maria, about 350 miles (550 km) northeast of Lima, told Reuters.
He denied a TV report that said six people had died -- two soldiers and four civilians -- when a column of about 200 rebels clashed with an army patrol.
Shining Path rebels have kept a low-profile since being upstaged by the daring assault on a cocktail party at the Japanese ambassador's home by their bitter rivals.
The government and MRTA rebels holding the diplomatic residence remained deadlocked on Tuesday as the 73 hostages spent their 35th day under the gun.
Both sides said they were ready to talk but a face-to-face meeting was on hold because the goverment ruled out considering the MRTA's main demand: the release of jailed comrades.
International Committee of the Red Cross representative Michel Minnig spent about three hours inside the besieged residence on Monday in what appeared to be a routine visit, witnesses said.

There has been little movement at the site since Friday when the MRTA freed a top security force chief for health reasons. It was the first hostage release in 17 days and one of a series of what the rebels have called "good-will gestures" since seizing hundreds of guests at the diplomatic reception.

Heavily-armed DINOES police patrolled within several yards (meters) of the high walls of the diplomatic compound. Witnesses said police have moved noticeably closer to the residence in recent days. The rebels have responded to previous troop movements outside the compound with bursts of warning shots.
Fujimori said the hostage crisis would cause a minimum of damage to the nation.

"Peru has converted itself into one of the region's most attractive emerging markets ... Investments in our country are totally guaranteed and the flow of investments has not stopped, proof that confidence in the country remains," he said.
Peruvian daily Expreso reported on Monday that MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini was communicating with fellow rebels throughout Peru via coded radio messages.

"The messages that are being sent from the radio, according to the police, are camouflaged through a system of binary numbers whose content is only know by Cerpa and the comrades backing him up from outside the residence," Expreso said, adding the code system was changed every week.

The remaining hostages inside the residence included about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, Peruvian government and security force officials, two ambassadors, and Fujimori's younger brother, Pedro.
